deep.lede: A master entrusts money to his servants, goes away, and returns to settle accounts. Matthew and Luke tell versions of the same parable that share its plot, its final proverb and the excuse of the fearful servant, but differ in nearly every number. Luke has also woven in a second, darker story about a king.

sections.heading: Talents and minas
sections.body:
Matthew's master gives {mt 25:15 πέντε τάλαντα} to one servant, two to another and one to a third, {mt 25:15 ἑκάστῳ κατὰ τὴν ἰδίαν δύναμιν} (“each according to his ability”). A talent was roughly fifteen to twenty years' wages, so these are vast sums. Luke's nobleman gives {lk 19:13 δέκα δούλους} (“ten servants”) one mina each, about three months' wages, with the instruction {lk 19:13 Πραγματεύσασθε ἐν ᾧ ἔρχομαι} (“do business until I come”). Only three of the ten are ever accounted for, a sign that Luke has adapted a three-servant story.

The English word “talent”, meaning a natural gift, comes from this parable, through medieval allegorical readings of Matthew's version.

sections.heading: The hard master
sections.body:
The third servant's excuse is nearly identical in both: the master reaps where he did not sow. Matthew's servant calls him {mt 25:24 σκληρὸς} (“hard”); Luke's calls him {lk 19:21 αὐστηρὸς} (“severe”), and adds a banking image: {lk 19:21 αἴρεις ὃ οὐκ ἔθηκας} (“you withdraw what you did not deposit”).

Both end with the same unsettling proverb: {mt 25:29 τῷ γὰρ ἔχοντι παντὶ δοθήσεται} (“to everyone who has, more will be given”), and {lk 19:26 παντὶ τῷ ἔχοντι δοθήσεται}. Mark has a version of the same saying in a different context (4:25), so it may have circulated on its own before being attached to this parable.

sections.heading: Luke's throne claimant
sections.body:
Luke's master is {lk 19:12 Ἄνθρωπός τις εὐγενὴς} (“a nobleman”) who goes to a distant country {lk 19:12 λαβεῖν ἑαυτῷ βασιλείαν} (“to receive a kingdom”). His citizens send a delegation after him: {lk 19:14 Οὐ θέλομεν τοῦτον βασιλεῦσαι ἐφ ἡμᾶς} (“we do not want this man to rule over us”). In 4 BCE, Herod's son Archelaus did exactly that, traveling to Rome to be confirmed as king while a Jewish delegation went to oppose him. Luke's audience may have recognized the history.

The story ends with the king ordering {lk 19:27 κατασφάξατε αὐτοὺς ἔμπροσθέν μου} (“slaughter them in front of me”). Luke places the parable just before Jesus enters Jerusalem, to correct those who thought {lk 19:11 παραχρῆμα μέλλει ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ ἀναφαίνεσθαι} (“the kingdom of God was about to appear immediately”). Matthew's rewards are joy ({mt 25:21 εἴσελθε εἰς τὴν χαρὰν τοῦ κυρίου σου}); Luke's are political: {lk 19:17 ἐξουσίαν ἔχων ἐπάνω δέκα πόλεων} (“authority over ten cities”).

deep.lede: The parable of the lost sheep appears in Matthew and Luke with the same hundred sheep and the same ninety-nine left behind, but in completely different settings. In Luke it defends Jesus' welcome of sinners against his critics. In Matthew it is pastoral advice to church leaders about straying members. The same story serves two different purposes.

sections.heading: Two audiences
sections.body:
Luke sets up the scene carefully: the Pharisees and scribes grumble, {lk 15:2 Οὗτος ἁμαρτωλοὺς προσδέχεται καὶ συνεσθίει αὐτοῖς} (“this man welcomes sinners and eats with them”). The parable is Jesus' answer, the first of three: a lost sheep, a lost coin and a lost son.

Matthew places it in a sermon on community life (chapter 18), addressed to the disciples. It follows the warning not to despise {mt 18:14 ἓν τῶν μικρῶν τούτων} (“one of these little ones”), and the parable ends with the Father's will that none of them should be lost. In Matthew's framing, the “little ones” are vulnerable believers, and the shepherds are church leaders.

sections.heading: Lost or straying?
sections.body:
The verbs differ. Matthew's sheep {mt 18:12 πλανηθῇ} (“goes astray”, wanders off); in Luke the man {lk 15:4 ἀπολέσας} (“has lost”) it. Matthew's shepherd searches with a conditional, {mt 18:13 ἐὰν γένηται εὑρεῖν αὐτό} (“**if** he finds it”). Luke's goes after it {lk 15:4 ἕως εὕρῃ αὐτό} (“**until** he finds it”). Luke's version contains no doubt about the outcome.

The ninety-nine are left {mt 18:12 ἐπὶ τὰ ὄρη} (“on the hills”) in Matthew, and {lk 15:4 ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ} (“in the wilderness”) in Luke. Either way, the shepherd takes a large risk for one sheep, and that is the point.

sections.heading: Joy in heaven
sections.body:
Luke elaborates the finding in ways that are typical of him. The shepherd puts the sheep {lk 15:5 ἐπὶ τοὺς ὤμους αὐτοῦ χαίρων} (“on his shoulders, rejoicing”), the image behind the earliest Christian art of the Good Shepherd, and calls friends and neighbors: {lk 15:6 Συγχάρητέ μοι} (“rejoice with me”). The moral is about repentance: {lk 15:7 χαρὰ ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ ἔσται ἐπὶ ἑνὶ ἁμαρτωλῷ μετανοοῦντι} (“there will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents”). That is ironic, since a sheep can't repent. The parable shows the shepherd's initiative; Luke's moral adds the language of his Gospel.

The Gospel of Thomas (saying 107) has a third version in which the lost sheep is “the largest” and the shepherd loves it more than the ninety-nine. That is an entirely different interpretation.

deep.lede: Jesus sends his disciples out to preach, with strict instructions about what not to take. This is one of the most complex knots in the Synoptic problem. Mark has one mission speech; Luke has two, one to the Twelve and one to the seventy; Matthew combines everything into one long discourse. And there are more than fifty minor agreements in this unit.

sections.heading: Staff and sandals
sections.body:
Mark lets the disciples take {mk 6:8 ῥάβδον μόνον} (“only a staff”) and tells them to wear {mk 6:9 ὑποδεδεμένους σανδάλια} (“sandals”). Matthew forbids both: {mt 10:10 μηδὲ ὑποδήματα μηδὲ ῥάβδον} (“no sandals, no staff”). Luke forbids the staff ({lk 9:3 μήτε ῥάβδον}) in the mission of the Twelve, and sandals in the mission of the seventy ({lk 10:4 μὴ ὑποδήματα}).

The staff is a clear minor agreement: Matthew and Luke both contradict Mark in the same way. The usual Two-Source explanation is that Q also contained a mission speech, a stricter one, and that Matthew and Luke both preferred its wording to Mark's. Luke's two missions, one following Mark and one following Q, support that idea. Farrer supporters see Luke simply following Matthew.

sections.heading: Only to Israel
sections.body: Matthew alone includes a startling restriction: {mt 10:5 Εἰς ὁδὸν ἐθνῶν μὴ ἀπέλθητε καὶ εἰς πόλιν Σαμαριτῶν μὴ εἰσέλθητε} (“do not go among the Gentiles or enter any Samaritan town”), but go {mt 10:6 πρὸς τὰ πρόβατα τὰ ἀπολωλότα οἴκου Ἰσραήλ} (“to the lost sheep of the house of Israel”). Matthew, the Gospel that ends with “make disciples of all nations”, preserves this saying that the more Gentile-oriented Luke leaves out. Many scholars think it reflects an early stage of the Jesus movement that Matthew kept in order to show a progression: first to Israel, then after the resurrection to all nations.

sections.heading: Sheep among wolves
sections.body:
The Q mission speech shares a memorable image: {mt 10:16 ἀποστέλλω ὑμᾶς ὡς πρόβατα ἐν μέσῳ λύκων} (“I send you out as sheep among wolves”). Luke's is {lk 10:3 ὡς ἄρνας} (“as **lambs**”), even more vulnerable. Matthew adds a proverb found nowhere else: {mt 10:16 γίνεσθε οὖν φρόνιμοι ὡς οἱ ὄφεις καὶ ἀκέραιοι ὡς αἱ περιστεραί} (“be wise as serpents and innocent as doves”).

Matthew's justification for not carrying provisions, {mt 10:10 ἄξιος γὰρ ὁ ἐργάτης τῆς τροφῆς αὐτοῦ} (“the worker deserves his food”), is quoted in 1 Timothy 5:18, in Luke's form (“wages”), right after a citation introduced as “scripture”. It may be one of the earliest signs of Gospel sayings becoming authoritative texts.

deep.lede: The feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle, apart from the resurrection, told in all four Gospels. That makes it the best single test case for how John relates to the Synoptics. The story is the same, but its setting, details and meaning are told in very different ways.

sections.heading: Sheep without a shepherd
sections.body:
Mark begins with Jesus' motive: {mk 6:34 ἐσπλαγχνίσθη ἐπ αὐτοὺς ὅτι ἦσαν ὡς πρόβατα μὴ ἔχοντα ποιμένα} (“he had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd”), a phrase from Numbers 27:17 and Ezekiel 34. The shepherd first feeds them by teaching. Then he tells the disciples {mk 6:37 Δότε αὐτοῖς ὑμεῖς φαγεῖν} (“**you** give them something to eat”), and they reply, perhaps sarcastically, that it would cost two hundred denarii.

The actions anticipate the Last Supper: {mk 6:41 λαβὼν} … {mk 6:41 εὐλόγησεν καὶ κατέκλασεν τοὺς ἄρτους καὶ ἐδίδου} (“taking … he blessed and broke the loaves and gave”). The same sequence of four actions, take, bless, break and give, recurs at the Last Supper (14:22).

sections.heading: Counting the crowd
sections.body: Mark says {mk 6:44 πεντακισχίλιοι ἄνδρες} (“five thousand **men**”), using the word for adult males. Luke follows ({lk 9:14 ὡσεὶ ἄνδρες πεντακισχίλιοι}). Only Matthew adds {mt 14:21 χωρὶς γυναικῶν καὶ παιδίων} (“besides women and children”). This might be meant to make the miracle larger, or to correct the impression that only men were present. In either case, Matthew has noticed what the source left out.

sections.heading: John: a boy, barley, and Passover
sections.body: John's version adds details found nowhere else. It is near Passover ({jn 6:4 ἦν δὲ ἐγγὺς τὸ πάσχα}). The food comes from {jn 6:9 παιδάριον ὧδε ὃς ἔχει πέντε ἄρτους κριθίνους} (“a boy here who has five **barley** loaves”), the bread of the poor. It also recalls 2 Kings 4:42–44, where Elisha feeds a hundred men with barley loaves and there are leftovers. Jesus {jn 6:11 εὐχαριστήσας} (“gave thanks”), the root of the word *eucharist*, and distributes the bread himself, with no disciples in between.

sections.heading: The sign and its meaning
sections.body:
In the Synoptics the miracle has no visible effect on the crowd. In John it causes a political crisis. The people say {jn 6:14 Οὗτός ἐστιν ἀληθῶς ὁ προφήτης} (“this is truly the Prophet”), the prophet like Moses of Deuteronomy 18. Then Jesus realizes they intend {jn 6:15 ἁρπάζειν αὐτὸν ἵνα ποιήσωσιν βασιλέα} (“to seize him to make him king”) and withdraws.

John then adds a long discourse (6:25–59) that reads the miracle as a sign: Jesus is the bread of life, the true manna. John usually calls miracles *sēmeia*, “signs”, which point beyond themselves. This scene shows how he takes a shared tradition and makes it the starting point for theology.

deep.lede: At Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asks his disciples who they say he is, and Peter answers. The scene is the turning point of Mark's Gospel. Each later evangelist expands Peter's answer, and Matthew adds the most consequential addition in the Synoptic tradition: the saying about the rock and the church.

sections.heading: Three versions of the answer
sections.body:
The question is almost the same in all three: {mk 8:29 Ὑμεῖς δὲ τίνα με λέγετε εἶναι} (“but who do you say that I am?”). The answer grows:

**Mark**: {mk 8:29 Σὺ εἶ ὁ χριστός} (“you are the Christ”).

**Luke**: {lk 9:20 Τὸν χριστὸν τοῦ θεοῦ} (“the Christ of God”).

**Matthew**: {mt 16:16 Σὺ εἶ ὁ χριστὸς ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ ζῶντος} (“you are the Christ, the Son of the living God”).

Matthew's question has also changed: {mt 16:13 Τίνα λέγουσιν οἱ ἄνθρωποι εἶναι τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου} (“who do people say **the Son of Man** is?”), so that Peter's answer equates the two titles.

sections.heading: Matthew's rock
sections.body:
Only Matthew has Jesus' response: {mt 16:17 Μακάριος εἶ Σίμων Βαριωνᾶ} (“blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah”), followed by {mt 16:18 σὺ εἶ Πέτρος καὶ ἐπὶ ταύτῃ τῇ πέτρᾳ οἰκοδομήσω μου τὴν ἐκκλησίαν} (“you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church”). The wordplay works in Greek (*Petros*/*petra*) and better still in Aramaic, where *kêpā* (Cephas) means “rock” for both.

The word *ekklēsia* (“church”) occurs in only two passages in all four Gospels, both in Matthew (here and 18:17). For that reason many critical scholars attribute the saying to Matthew's church rather than to Jesus. Others argue for an early Aramaic origin. Interpretations have divided Christianity: Catholic tradition sees the rock as Peter and his successors; many Protestant readers have taken it to be Peter's confession, or Christ himself.

sections.heading: Mark's silence, and John's Peter
sections.body:
Mark's Jesus neither praises nor rejects Peter's answer. He just {mk 8:30 ἐπετίμησεν αὐτοῖς ἵνα μηδενὶ λέγωσιν περὶ αὐτοῦ} (“strictly warned them to tell no one about him”). Mark uses the same verb, *epitimaō* (“rebuke”), a few verses later when Peter rebukes Jesus, and Jesus rebukes Peter as “Satan”. Peter has the right title but the wrong idea of what it means.

John's nearest equivalent comes after the Bread of Life discourse, when many followers leave. Peter says {jn 6:68 Κύριε πρὸς τίνα ἀπελευσόμεθα ῥήματα ζωῆς αἰωνίου ἔχεις} (“Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life”) and confesses {jn 6:69 σὺ εἶ ὁ ἅγιος τοῦ θεοῦ} (“you are the Holy One of God”). This is the same title a demon uses in Mark 1:24.

deep.lede: How did Peter come to follow Jesus? Mark tells it in five verses: an invitation by the lake and an immediate response. Luke turns it into a miracle story with a huge catch of fish. John has a strikingly similar miracle, but places it **after** the resurrection. The overlap raises one of the most interesting questions about how John relates to the Synoptics.

sections.heading: Mark: the bare call
sections.body: In Mark, Jesus sees Simon and Andrew {mk 1:16 ἀμφιβάλλοντας ἐν τῇ θαλάσσῃ} (“casting a net in the sea”) and says {mk 1:17 Δεῦτε ὀπίσω μου καὶ ποιήσω ὑμᾶς γενέσθαι ἁλιεῖς ἀνθρώπων} (“follow me, and I will make you become fishers of people”). They respond with no explanation: {mk 1:18 καὶ εὐθὺς ἀφέντες τὰ δίκτυα ἠκολούθησαν αὐτῷ} (“and immediately they left their nets and followed him”). Mark offers no psychology and no previous meeting, only the authority of Jesus' word. Matthew copies almost all of it, with 64% shared wording.

sections.heading: Luke: the miraculous catch
sections.body:
Luke delays the call to chapter 5 and gives Peter a reason to follow. After a fruitless night, Simon says {lk 5:5 Ἐπιστάτα δι ὅλης νυκτὸς κοπιάσαντες οὐδὲν ἐλάβομεν} (“Master, we worked all night and caught nothing”), but obeys, and the nets begin to break. Peter falls at Jesus' knees: {lk 5:8 Ἔξελθε ἀπ ἐμοῦ ὅτι ἀνὴρ ἁμαρτωλός εἰμι κύριε} (“go away from me, for I am a sinful man, Lord”). The address changes from *Epistata* (“master”) to *Kyrie* (“Lord”).

The commission is reworded too: {lk 5:10 ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν ἀνθρώπους ἔσῃ ζωγρῶν} (“from now on you will be catching people **alive**”). The verb *zōgreō* means to take alive, as prisoners were taken in war, rather than to catch fish for food.

sections.heading: John 21: the same miracle, after Easter
sections.body:
At the end of John, seven disciples have fished all night and caught nothing. A stranger on shore tells them to cast to the right side, and the net is so full {jn 21:6 οὐκέτι αὐτὸ ἑλκύσαι ἴσχυον ἀπὸ τοῦ πλήθους τῶν ἰχθύων} (“they could no longer haul it in because of the number of fish”). Peter drags the net ashore with {jn 21:11 ἑκατὸν πεντήκοντα τριῶν} (“a hundred fifty-three”) fish, and {jn 21:11 οὐκ ἐσχίσθη τὸ δίκτυον} (“the net was not torn”), unlike Luke's net, which was tearing.

The shared skeleton is unmistakable: a fruitless night, a command from Jesus, a huge catch, a net under strain, and Peter at the center. Did Luke move a resurrection story back into Jesus' ministry, or did John's tradition move a ministry story forward? Scholars are divided. The number 153 has inspired many symbolic interpretations, from Augustine's arithmetic to Jerome's claim that it was the number of known species of fish. None has won general agreement.

deep.lede: A Roman officer asks Jesus to heal his servant from a distance, and Jesus marvels at his faith. Matthew and Luke share this story with a striking level of verbal agreement in the dialogue, yet they disagree completely about how the conversation took place. John has a related story of a royal official and his son.

sections.heading: Words that match
sections.body: The centurion's speech is nearly identical in the two Gospels: {mt 8:8 Κύριε οὐκ εἰμὶ ἱκανὸς ἵνα μου ὑπὸ τὴν στέγην εἰσέλθῃς} and {lk 7:6 οὐ γὰρ ἱκανός εἰμι ἵνα ὑπὸ τὴν στέγην μου εἰσέλθῃς} (“I am not worthy to have you come under my roof”). Jesus' response matches too: {mt 8:10 παρ οὐδενὶ τοσαύτην πίστιν ἐν τῷ Ἰσραὴλ εὗρον} and {lk 7:9 οὐδὲ ἐν τῷ Ἰσραὴλ τοσαύτην πίστιν εὗρον} (“not even in Israel have I found such faith”). The centurion's words are still repeated in the Catholic Mass before Communion. This is one of the few miracle stories in Q, which was mostly a collection of sayings, and it is the dialogue that is preserved precisely.

sections.heading: Face to face, or through messengers?
sections.body:
In Matthew the centurion comes to Jesus himself. In Luke he never meets Jesus. He first sends {lk 7:3 πρεσβυτέρους τῶν Ἰουδαίων} (“elders of the Jews”), who vouch for him: {lk 7:4 Ἄξιός ἐστιν} (“he is worthy”), {lk 7:5 ἀγαπᾷ γὰρ τὸ ἔθνος ἡμῶν καὶ τὴν συναγωγὴν αὐτὸς ᾠκοδόμησεν ἡμῖν} (“for he loves our nation, and he built our synagogue”). Then he sends {lk 7:6 φίλους} (“friends”) to say he is **not** worthy.

Luke's version anticipates the story of Cornelius in Acts 10, a God-fearing centurion who gives alms to the Jewish people. Luke may have shaped this story to set a pattern for welcoming Gentiles: through Jewish mediation, and with humility. Augustine harmonized the two versions by noting that one acts through one's agents. Modern scholars mostly see two editorial choices.

sections.heading: Matthew's warning
sections.body: Matthew uses the story to warn his readers, adding a saying that Luke places elsewhere (13:28–29): {mt 8:11 πολλοὶ ἀπὸ ἀνατολῶν καὶ δυσμῶν ἥξουσιν} (“many will come from east and west”) to recline with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, while {mt 8:12 οἱ δὲ υἱοὶ τῆς βασιλείας ἐκβληθήσονται} (“the sons of the kingdom will be thrown out”). Gentile faith exposes insider complacency, which is one of Matthew's recurring themes.

sections.heading: John's royal official
sections.body: John 4 tells of a {jn 4:46 βασιλικὸς} (“royal official”), probably in Herod Antipas' service, whose {jn 4:46 υἱὸς} (“son”) is ill in Capernaum. Jesus heals at a distance with a word: {jn 4:50 Πορεύου ὁ υἱός σου ζῇ} (“go, your son lives”). The healing happens at the same hour, as in Matthew ({mt 8:13 ἐν τῇ ὥρᾳ ἐκείνῃ}). Matthew's word for the patient, {mt 8:8 ὁ παῖς μου}, can mean either “my servant” or “my boy”. Luke has {lk 7:3 τὸν δοῦλον αὐτοῦ} (“his slave”) and John “son”, so the ambiguous *pais* may be where the versions diverged.
